title: The Basics at the Table
subtitle: Six sessions for the brand new believer, with every churchy word earned before it is used
summary: Church has a vocabulary problem. We say gospel, grace, baptism, communion, testimony, and forget that these words are a foreign language to the person who just came through the door. This study assumes nothing. Six sessions around a table walk a new believer through the things that hold a life: what the gospel actually announces, how to pray without performing, how to read the Bible without fear, why you cannot do this alone, what baptism and the Supper are, and how to tell your own story plainly. Every churchy word gets earned before it gets used. By the end, the new believer is not fluent in church. They are grounded in Christ, which is better.
setting: A kitchen table, a booth, a porch. Two people or a few. No stage, no jargon, no assumed knowledge.
forWho: The brand new believer, the returner who never learned the foundations, and the friend walking beside either one.
rhythm: Six sessions, about an hour. Weekly is best while the concrete is still wet.
leaderNote: Watch your mouth, in the kindest sense. Every time a church word slips out unexplained, the new believer quietly decides this world has a members only language, and a wall goes up. So slow down and earn each word: say what it meant before it became furniture. Never make them feel behind for asking what something means. The question is the whole point of the table. And go first in honesty every time, because a new believer learns whether faith can be honest by watching whether yours is.

sessions.title: The News Itself
sessions.bigIdea: Gospel is an old word for news, an announcement that something has happened. Christianity is not advice about becoming good. It is news about what God has done, and news is received, not achieved.
sessions.open: Tell each other about the best news you ever received. Who told you, and what did you do the moment you heard it?
sessions.read: Start with the word itself. Gospel translates an old Greek word that meant a herald's announcement, the news of a victory or a new king. Now read 1 Corinthians 15:1-8, where Paul writes down the announcement he received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared to named, living witnesses. Then read Romans 5:6-8. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
observe: Paul lists the gospel as a set of events. Name them in order. Notice how few of them are instructions.
In Romans, when did Christ die for us, before or after we got ourselves together? What exact words does Paul use?
talk: Advice says do this and you might be accepted. News says this was done and you are accepted. Which one have you been treating Christianity as, and where did you learn that version?
While we were still sinners. What does that timing do to the fear that God is waiting for a better version of you?
If the gospel is finished news, why do you think so many of us keep trying to earn what has already been announced?
sessions.practice: Once a day this week, say the news to yourself in one plain sentence: Christ died for my sins, was buried, and was raised, and it was done while I was still a mess. Say it until it stops sounding like someone else's mail.
sessions.send: You are not the worker on this project. You are the one the news came for. Start there every morning.
sessions.passItOn: Practice saying the gospel out loud to your table partner in your own words, one minute, no church language. If your grandmother and your barber could both follow it, you have it.

sessions.title: Talking to God Without Performing
sessions.bigIdea: Prayer is not a religious skill you lack. It is a child talking to a Father, and the disciples who asked Jesus how to do it were handed something short, plain, and repeatable.
sessions.open: What has stopped you from praying so far? Not knowing the words, feeling like a fraud, wondering if anyone is listening? Name it plainly.
sessions.read: Read Luke 11:1-13. Grown men who had prayed all their lives watched Jesus pray and asked him to teach them, so nobody at this table should be embarrassed to be a beginner. Jesus gives them a prayer a child can memorize: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation. Then he tells them to ask, seek, and knock, because the Father gives good gifts to those who ask him.
observe: The prayer Jesus teaches is only a few lines. What does it ask for, and what does it noticeably not bother with?
In the story of the friend at midnight and the father giving gifts, what is Jesus saying about the one being asked?
talk: Jesus starts with Father, not with a title you have to be qualified to use. What changes if prayer is a family conversation rather than a formal appointment?
Daily bread is groceries, gas money, the ordinary stuff. Does it surprise you that Jesus tells you to pray about things that small? What have you assumed was too minor to bring?
Forgive us, as we forgive. Prayer and how you treat people are wired together in this prayer. Where does that press on you right now?
sessions.practice: Pray once a day this week, out loud if you can, two minutes, using the Lord's Prayer as your outline: Father, your kingdom, my bread, my forgiveness, my protection. Badly counts. Showing up is the whole assignment.
sessions.send: God is not grading your grammar. He is a Father glad his child came to talk. Come daily.
sessions.passItOn: Before you leave tonight, pray one sentence out loud with your table partner. One sentence. The person who can pray simply in front of one friend will one day teach another beginner to pray.

sessions.title: Reading the Bible Without Fear
sessions.bigIdea: The Bible is a library you will spend a lifetime in, not a test you can fail this week. Start small, start in a Gospel, and expect the God who wrote it to meet you in it.
sessions.open: Be honest about the Bible. Intimidating, boring, confusing, precious, unknown? What is your history with this book, even if the history is none?
sessions.read: First, get the shape of the thing. The Bible is not one book but sixty six, written across centuries, history and poetry and letters and Gospels, all telling one story that lands on Jesus. Nobody starts by understanding all of it, including your pastor. Now read Psalm 119:103-105. How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. Then read Isaiah 55:10-11, where God says his word is like rain and snow that water the earth. It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose.
observe: The psalmist calls the word a lamp to my feet, not a floodlight over the whole road. How much does a lamp at your feet actually show you?
In Isaiah, whose job is it to make the word do its work, the reader's or God's?
talk: Many people quit the Bible because they started at page one and died somewhere in Leviticus. What would it mean to read for the next step instead of the whole map?
Sweeter than honey is an experience, not a duty. Have you ever tasted anything like that in reading, any book? What would it take to expect it here?
What is your biggest fear about reading the Bible on your own, getting it wrong, finding something you do not like, or finding nothing at all? Say it at the table.
sessions.practice: Read the Gospel of Mark this week, one chapter a day for six days. It is the shortest Gospel, written for beginners. Before each chapter, ask God to speak. After, write one sentence: what did I see? Bring your sentences next time.
sessions.send: You do not need to master the book. You need to be in it, a little, daily, and let it do its slow work. A lamp for tonight's step is enough.
sessions.passItOn: Show one person this week, maybe a family member, how you are doing it: which book, how much, what you ask first. Reading Scripture is caught from watching someone ordinary do it.

sessions.title: Why You Need a Body
sessions.bigIdea: Church is not a building you attend or a show you review. It is a body you belong to, and a severed hand does not stay alive on its own sincerity.
sessions.open: Where in your life have you been part of something you genuinely could not have done alone, a team, a crew, a family holding a crisis? What did the others carry that you could not?
sessions.read: Earn the word first. Church in the New Testament never means a building. It translates a word that means the assembly, the gathered people. Now read 1 Corinthians 12:12-20. Just as the body is one and has many members, so it is with Christ. The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Then read Hebrews 10:24-25. Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another.
observe: Paul's picture is a body, not an audience or a club. What can a body part do that a spectator cannot, and what happens to it when separated?
Hebrews says meeting together exists to stir up and encourage. Who is doing that work in the room, the professionals or everyone?
talk: Plenty of people say they can follow Jesus alone, and often a church hurt them into saying it. What is understandable in that, and what does the body picture say it costs?
You are a member, which in Paul's language means a body part with a function, not a name on a roster. What might you be for a body, a hand, an ear, a spine? What do you naturally give a room?
What would you need from a church to actually let yourself be known there, not just seated there?
sessions.practice: Attend a gathering of the church this week, and do one thing beyond attending: learn one person's name and one true thing about their life. You are not evaluating a performance. You are meeting your body.
sessions.send: Nobody follows Jesus alone for long. You were saved into a family. Go be locatable in it.
sessions.passItOn: Bring someone with you. The empty seat next to you in a gathering is the easiest invitation you will ever make: come sit with me.

sessions.title: The Water and the Meal
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus left his people two physical signs, baptism and the Supper. One marks the beginning, once, like a wedding. The other feeds the life, over and over, like the marriage.
sessions.open: Why do we mark the biggest moments of life with physical ceremonies, rings, vows, birthday candles, handshakes? What does the body-and-object part do that words alone cannot?
sessions.read: Two words to earn tonight. Baptism comes from a word that means to plunge or immerse. Communion, which some churches call the Lord's Supper, is the shared meal Jesus started on the night he was betrayed. Read Romans 6:3-4. We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. Then read Luke 22:19-20. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them, saying, this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.
observe: In Romans, baptism acts out a burial and a rising. Whose death and resurrection is the new believer being joined to?
At the table, what does Jesus say the bread and the cup are given for, and what one thing does he command the meal to do?
talk: Baptism does not make God love you, any more than a wedding creates the love. So what is it for? What happens when a private promise is made in public, in front of witnesses?
The Supper is a meal you receive, not a performance you give. Why do you think Jesus chose eating, the most ordinary act there is, as the way his people remember him?

Faithful churches practice these two signs somewhat differently, who is baptized and when, how often the meal is shared, and they are still one family. What questions do you want to ask about how your church does it?
sessions.practice: If you have not been baptized, talk to your pastor or your table partner this week about taking that step, and ask every question you have. If you have been, write down what you would want a watching friend to understand about the next Supper you receive.
sessions.send: He gave you water for the once and bread for the always. Neither one is magic. Both are him keeping his promises where your body can feel them.
sessions.passItOn: Baptisms are public on purpose. When yours comes, or the next one at your church does, invite someone far from God to come watch. The sign was designed to be seen.

sessions.title: Telling Your Story
sessions.bigIdea: You do not need a degree to bear witness. The man born blind had one unanswerable sentence: though I was blind, now I see. You have one too, and somebody needs to hear it.
sessions.open: Look back over these six weeks together. What is one thing that is different in you, even slightly, from the day you started?
sessions.read: One last word to earn. Church people say testimony, which just means what a witness says, what you saw and what happened to you. Read John 9:13-25. A man born blind is healed by Jesus and then interrogated by experts who want him to denounce the healer. He refuses to argue theology with them and stands on what he knows: whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see. Then read 1 Peter 3:15. In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. Peter adds in the next breath that it is done with gentleness and respect.
observe: The healed man is questioned by people with far more training than he has. What does he admit he does not know, and what does he refuse to let go of?
Peter assumes people will ask about your hope. What must a life look like before neighbors start asking that question?
talk: You cannot argue everyone's objections, and John 9 says you do not have to. What is your though I was blind, now I see, the before and after only you can report?
Gentleness and respect rule out winning arguments and cornering people. What does it look like to tell your story so the listener stays free?
Who in your life has already noticed something changing in you? What would you say if they asked this week?
sessions.practice: Write your story this week in three short parts, what life was, what happened, what is different now, in under two minutes and with no church vocabulary you have not earned. Tell it to your table partner before you tell anyone else.
sessions.send: Six weeks ago the words were foreign. Now you can say the news, pray plainly, open the book, belong to a body, receive the signs, and tell what you saw. That is not graduation. That is a foundation.
sessions.passItOn: Somewhere near you is a person as new as you were six weeks ago, or about to be. Take them through this study. You are not the expert at their table. You are the friend who is six weeks ahead, which is exactly what they need.
